records.example: With a symbolic checker ahead of the judge, 81 math questions run 3 times each scored the same every time, with 0 regressions in 486 evaluations.
records.detail: The question evaluator used in the AP work added a math checker because a model judge could score the same compound-interest question 1.0 in one run and 0.0 in the next. records.against: the step that turns an item into something the checker can compute can misrepresent the problem, so the judge may still override an "incorrect" verdict, and the measured gain was 3 net improvements. Filing format faults under alignment is what the judge's rubric asked for: it asks whether the format is correct and fails curriculum alignment if not, though that rubric file postdates the run. Where a code check rests on a model's own extraction, the same evaluator leaves the judge free: a math check's finding of an error may be overridden because "the extraction step can sometimes misrepresent the problem", and a picture check may lift a fail while its contradictions stay advisory. records.title: Test fit against the official scope
records.statement: Test a question's fit to the curriculum by checking that the unit's official scope can answer it.
records.detail: A study summarised in the AP question work measured validity partly with a question-answering test, on the view that a curriculum-aligned question should be answerable using the curriculum's own scope definition, alongside similarity to the official curriculum (`icloud-work/ML learnings/research_educational_content_generation.md`). With that yardstick, grounding generation in official curriculum documents took validity from 12-15% to 92-96% with the same generator. That result is about grounding, so it shows the test in use, not that the test is valid.
records.against: The test's own accuracy is not reported; it was the yardstick, not the thing tested. The study covers one other subject, secondary mathematics (`icloud-work/ML learnings/research_educational_content_generation.md`, line 276).

evidence.quote: **How validity is measured:** Semantic Textual Similarity against official curriculum + RAG-QA test (a curriculum-aligned question should be answerable using the curriculum's own scope definition). This is analogous to our curriculum_alignment dimension.

RAG methods go from 12-15% validity to 92-96% validity by grounding generation in official curriculum documents. The study uses GPT-4o as the generator for all conditions — the variable is retrieval, not the model.

citations.ref: Automated Generation of Curriculum-Aligned MCQs for Malaysian Secondary Mathematics (arXiv:2508.04442)

records.title: A repeating failure is a fault to find
records.statement: Treat a failure that repeats across items, a whole type at zero or all passing, or scores bunched under the pass line as a specific fault, not noise: rule out a broken pipeline or measurement, read the failing items for the cause, and test it before choosing a fix.
records.example: Nine targeted fixes, each for one specific fault, added 15.1 points to the pass rate.
records.detail: At 81.9% the AP question work's remaining failures were systematic, not random (`icloud-work/ML learnings/gemini_benchmark_relentless.md`). Of about 40-50 automated iterations most changed nothing, and the nine that worked each removed a specific code or prompt bug behind a specific failing dimension, adding 15.1 points in about 48 hours. The project's diagnostic method goes from the aggregate to the failing dimension and items, then two or three hypotheses and a test that tells them apart, with a catalogue of signatures: a whole unit failing points to wrong scope labels, a whole item type to missing examples, right content on the wrong topic to an ignored constraint, and wrong specifics to invented details (`icloud-work/ML learnings/debugging_methodology.md`). Each time a step was skipped, going from an aggregate straight to a fix, a training run was wasted.
records.against: A repeating failure is not always fixable in the instructions: "The failure is at the weight level, not the prompt level." (`icloud-work/ML learnings/prompt_engineering_deep_dive.md`, line 73), and the same source's last 3% were random slips (`icloud-work/ML learnings/gemini_benchmark_relentless.md`, line 208). A whole item type once failed because of a routing fault, not missing examples (`icloud-work/ML learnings/sft_v7_benchmark_postmortem.md`, line 26), and even with the method the first hypotheses were often wrong (`icloud-work/ML learnings/stage2_postmortem_full.md`, line 180). The none-or-all rule is stated from one incident, not measured across runs: "**NOT re-verified by me on disk this turn; this is the directive's framing, not new measurement.**" (~/Library/Mobile Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/work/aptraining/workspace/comms/_deprecated/outboxes/from_research/2026-05-01T1300Z_R44_eval_phantom_class.md, 32). The reading of bunched scores rests on one item type in two runs. Inferred from counts: the reports never cross-tabulate rule by item type. In both runs the hard-fail count equals the fill-in count (18 and 16), and the sampled hard-fail examples are all fill-in items. The review's own caveat: drift in the judge over the window can't be fully excluded, so per-version rates should be re-confirmed on one pinned judge version.

evidence.quote: At 81.9%, the system was generating correct AP questions most of the time. The remaining ~18% failures were not random — they were systematic, patterned failures. The key insight that drove the relentless push: every failure is evidence of a specific, fixable bug.
**Total:** 15.1 percentage point improvement from 9 targeted fixes over ~48 hours.

records.title: Size output caps from real outputs
records.statement: Size any output length cap from the longest real outputs plus headroom, and check that every delivered item is complete, because a cap or a timeout can cut an item short without an error.
records.example: A timed-out call returned an empty or truncated item, which scored 0.0.
records.detail: The AP question work's synthesis blamed missing answer choices and incomplete output on a borderline output cap of 8192 for question sets, citing vendor guidance that a cap below the worst-case length truncates output silently (`icloud-work/ML learnings/master_strategy_apr24.md`). Its research summary advises profiling the longest outputs per question type and adding a 20-30% buffer (`icloud-work/ML learnings/research_qwen3_structured_multistage.md`). Separately, a timeout returned an empty or truncated response that scored 0.0, and a completeness check that counts opening against closing braces was added after the call (`icloud-work/ML learnings/gemini_benchmark_relentless.md`).
records.against: Whether caps caused the missing answer choices is unsettled: after a smaller writer's caps were cut, the record says "No quality regression observed after the reduction" (`icloud-work/ML learnings/pipeline_architecture_insight.md`, line 70). The project's own rule can set a cap below the worst case: "Run 5 DBQ requests, find where timeouts start, set limit at 50% of that." (the same file, line 73).

evidence.quote: - **Never set `max_tokens` below the worst-case full output length.** For complex AP exam questions with 5+ nested fields, estimate the maximum possible output and add a 20-30% buffer.

**Practical recommendation:** Profile your longest outputs per question type before setting token limits. Add 30% headroom. For mcq_set (3 questions + stimulus), 8192 is probably borderline — consider 12000-16000.
**Result of timeout:** The generator returned an empty or truncated response. Score: 0.0.

**Fix:** Added JSON truncation detection after the Pro call:
1. Check if the response JSON is complete (count opening vs closing braces)

Missing answer choices, incomplete JSON. Root cause: **token limit truncation** — Alibaba Cloud docs explicitly warn that capping `max_tokens` below worst-case output causes silently truncated JSON. Our `mcq_set_questions` limit of 8192 is borderline. Secondary cause: SFT loss doesn't shape partial schema correctness.

records.title: Verified facts as the only source
records.statement: Give a writer verified facts and real sources, quoted into its instructions, as the only source it may draw on rather than as inspiration, because from memory or its own research it invents dates, documents and claims.

records.title: Warnings and bans don't steer a writer
records.statement: Warnings and bans in a prompt don't reliably steer a writer and can bring on the error they name, so change what it is given instead: the material it may use, hard limits on it, and how the item is built.
records.example: Adding 'be careful' warnings took a prompt's pass rate from 45% to 30%.
records.detail: In a prompt sweep with 20 items per variant, adding 'be careful' warnings gave a 30% pass rate against the baseline's 45%, with factual accuracy at 60% in both (`icloud-work/ML learnings/prompt_engineering_deep_dive.md`); the project's reading is that warnings without actual constraints just introduce hedging (`icloud-work/ML learnings/failures_and_false_starts.md`). Bans did no better on fine-tuned models: told not to use specific facts, one used wrong specific facts instead of right ones (`icloud-work/ML learnings/sft_v7_benchmark_postmortem.md`). Another, ordered in capitals not to write about any other topic, went on writing about the wrong topic (`icloud-work/ML learnings/stage2_postmortem_full.md`).
records.against: a large model mostly respected a ban on listing specific evidence; the note calls that instruction good enough for a large model and insufficient for a 14B one (`icloud-work/ML learnings/sft_v7_benchmark_postmortem.md`). a large model mostly respected a ban on listing specific evidence, and the notes conclude that an instruction good enough for a large model is not enough for a 14B one. Both cases involve one small model, and the analysis ties the failure to its weak factual memory, so the finding may not carry to larger writers (`icloud-work/aptraining/.agent/research/failure_taxonomy.md`); whether the later fix worked is not recorded there. The same postmortem proposes hard negatives, the model's own off-topic outputs labelled as rejected, as a fix, and the falsified run's next step pairs real sources against the model's own weakest samples; neither was measured here, and both use real outputs rather than made-up faults. none found; the comparison rests on 11 sets.

evidence.quote: **Method:** test_variants.py — 9 variants, N=20 each, APUSH Unit 7
| baseline | 45% | 60% | Standard prompt |
| caution | 30% | 60% | Added "be careful" warnings |

**The "caution" variant also failed:** Adding "be careful" warnings about factual accuracy produced 30% pass rate — worse than anything. Warnings that tell the model to be careful without giving it actual constraints just introduce hedging behavior. The model starts prefacing with qualifications instead of generating confident content.

**Why it doesn't work:** The model ignores negative constraints. It has strong parametric associations (France → exploration → Protestant → Huguenots → plausible but wrong) that override the instruction. Telling the model "don't use specific facts" just means it uses wrong specific facts instead of right ones.
DO NOT write about any other topic.
**Result:** Failures persisted.

records.title: Model judges score higher than people
records.statement: Don't take a model judge's scores for a person's: model judges can score the same educational responses higher than human raters do, as all four did for all five systems in one benchmark, and agree with people only in part.
records.example: In one published benchmark, all 20 model-judge averages were above the human average for the same model.
records.detail: A published benchmark of language models in teaching scenarios, bundled with one project's evaluator, reports model-judge and human scores for the same responses (`icloud-work/incept/incept-multilingual-generation/src/evaluator/EduBench/README.md`). In its scenario-level table each of four model judges gives each of five models a higher average than people do, for example 8.46 from one judge against 7.50 from people for the smallest model. The coefficient of concordance between people and each model judge is 0.56 to 0.63, and the authors note that the model evaluations do not fully align with human judgments. It is one reason to score a model judge on person-labelled cases before trusting its level.
records.against: The rankings agree at the extremes: people put the same models best and worst as the model judges do, 'which are consistent with the model-based evaluation results' (`icloud-work/incept/incept-multilingual-generation/src/evaluator/EduBench/README.md`, line 193). People also agree with the model judges about as well as the model judges agree with each other, 0.55 to 0.65, which the authors call strong agreement. The benchmark reports the same best and worst systems under the human raters and the model judges, and it calls model-to-model W values of the same size, 0.55 to 0.65, strong agreement (`icloud-work/inceptbench/submodules/EduBench/README.md`, L193 and L217).

records.title: Reasoning or score
records.statement: Whether a judge's own reasoning should be allowed to overrule its failing score, since an item's explanation can steer that reasoning toward a pass; the effect has not been isolated.
records.detail: The judge's instructions include an anti-contradiction step: when its reasoning concludes the content is correct but a score is 0.0, it must change the score to 1.0. An adversarial reading argues that because the judge writes its reasoning before the score is applied, an item explanation templated to read as correct can force a score of 1.0, and proposes letting the rule fire only between the overall score and the individual metrics. No run in the files read isolates the rule's effect. To settle it: score the same items with and without the per-metric rule, against verdicts a person has checked.
records.against: Items that carried the mirror-style explanation the reading blames, under an authority-framed source, still passed only 4 of 10, so the explanation alone did not force passes: "Result: 4/10 = 40% pass vs. 2/2 = 100% on the no-stimulus control on the same content." (~/Library/Mobile Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/work/aptraining/Cheater/reports/DEAD_HYPOTHESES.md, 9-10)

evidence.quote: But because the judge writes reasoning BEFORE the score is applied, a template-driven explanation that prefills the judge's reasoning toward "content is correct" will force the score to 1.0 even when the judge's gut would have failed it.
**Patch:** the self-heal rule should fire ONLY in the overall-score-vs-individual-metric direction (the original intent), not in the per-metric direction.
Result: 4/10 = 40% pass vs. 2/2 = 100% on the no-stimulus control on the same content.

records.title: Known faults fail by default
records.statement: A judge that passes whatever is arguable talks itself past known faults: give each one a narrow check that fails by default, name the excuses it has used as invalid, and accept an override only when it quotes the exception it relies on.

records.against: The 94% run covered a whole pull request (#268) that also changed other parts of the evaluator, and the two-item result shipped three changes together, so the effect of the excuse list alone is unknown. records.title: Explanations must fit the item given
records.statement: Explanations, hints and feedback must be true of the item as given: an explanation is written for the options' final order and backs the keyed option and no other, which code checks and fails when it can't tell, and a judge checks every other claim they make against the item itself.
records.example: A judge scored factual accuracy 1.0 on an item whose explanation wrongly called a wrong option a fact stated explicitly in the text.
records.detail: In one reported case the judge scored factual accuracy 1.0 on an inference item whose explanation called a wrong option 'a fact stated explicitly in the text' when that claim was not in the passage, because it accepted the explanation's description of itself without checking (`icloud-work/inceptbench-main/tests/test_evaluator_prompt_rules_967.py`). The reading and writing rules now make the judge verify such labels against the passage, and the ELA rules forbid using the explanation as the sole source of truth (`icloud-work/inceptbench-main/src/inceptbench/prompts/question/sat_rw_evaluation.txt`; `icloud-work/inceptbench-main/src/inceptbench/prompts/question/ela_evaluation.txt`). The closed-ended rubric treats explanations, hints, feedback templates and diagnostic notes as part of the content and fails an item whose support text discusses values that are not among its options, counting it under clarity rather than accuracy when code has confirmed the answer (`icloud-work/inceptbench-main/src/inceptbench/prompts/question/closed_ended_evaluation.txt`).
records.against: Each experiment had 10 items, and three different fixes each passed 10 of 10, among them a shuffle in code that rewrote every letter reference and a self-check instruction, so keeping the letters in sync matters more than the order of the steps (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/docs/archive/EXPERIMENT_RESULTS_2026-02-18.md`). A pattern check catches only explicit letter phrases: an explanation can argue for a wrong option without naming it (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/python/benchmark_runs/analysis_iter1.md`).

evidence.quote: The evaluator accepted the explanation's self-characterization without checking.

**Rule:** When an explanation claims a distractor is "a fact stated explicitly in the text" or "explicitly stated," you MUST verify whether the *specific claim made in that distractor* is literally present in the stimulus.
Do NOT use `answer_explanation` as your sole source of truth — the explanation may be absent, wrong, or misleading.

records.title: Judge difficulty for the target learners
records.statement: Judge an item's difficulty for its target learners by comparing it with validated items for their grade, weighing the inference it demands and the strength of its wrong options, not by a model's direct rating or simulated learners, because a model can't simulate not knowing and so underrates difficulty.
records.example: The reading-question check compares a candidate with the 5 most similar validated questions for its grade.
records.detail: The AP work's evaluator notes in its matching rubric that a task which feels obvious in hindsight to someone who knows the subject is still diagnostically useful if the target students are learning the concept, and fails one only when there is no plausible confusion for the intended grade (`icloud-work/inceptbench-main/src/inceptbench/prompts/question/match_evaluation.txt`). The reading-question pipeline bundled with it judges whether a question suits its grade by comparing it with the 5 most semantically similar validated questions for that grade (`icloud-work/inceptbench/submodules/reading-question-qc/qc_pipeline/config/prompts.json`), and runs that check only when benchmark questions are supplied (`icloud-work/inceptbench/submodules/reading-question-qc/qc_pipeline/README.md`). Both are design choices; no measurement of either was found.
records.against: The check runs only when benchmark items are supplied: "- Question QC with both keys + --examples: 10-11 checks (adds too-close and difficulty)" (`icloud-work/incept/incept-multilingual-generation/src/external_submodules/reading-question-qc/qc_pipeline/README.md`, line 236). The feature study itself calls direct estimates moderately to strongly correlated with true difficulty, and worse for early grades (Razavi & Powers 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08804); the BrainLift calls its r ≈ 0.4–0.6 a rough summary across studies that depends on domain, grade and prompt design (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0163-cold-start-item-difficulty-estimation.qmd`). Simulated students aligned with DPO and calibrated with IRT outperform other simulation approaches, and the BrainLift still finds simulation useful as a supplementary signal (Scarlatos et al. 2025, as reported in `~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/feedback/feedback3/WF - Assessment  Feedback Brain - 260624-200115.md`, line 3206); and a predictor framing, rather than role-play, reached r≈0.72–0.79 at population level (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/generator-insights.md`, lines 123-124).

evidence.quote: **NOTE**: A task that feels "obvious in hindsight" to an expert is still diagnostically useful if the target student population is learning the concept.

records.title: Don't rehearse the test you validate against
records.statement: When validating a new measure against an established test, don't let it act as practice for that test: give it only after the official sitting, or counterbalance the order and report the practice effect.
records.example: In one validation plan about half the cohort sits the official test first, which gives a linking estimate with no prior exposure to the new test.
records.detail: An adversarial review of a reading assessment's validity plan pointed out that giving the new test days before the official one would be a practice intervention on the very test it was being validated against (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/red-team/RED_TEAM_FINDINGS.md`). The plan has every student take both tests within two weeks in counterbalanced order, so the half that sits the official test first gives a linking estimate with no prior exposure, and it offers an arm that gives the new test only after the official sitting (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/validity/04_CONCURRENT_VALIDITY_PLAN.md`). Counterbalancing measures the practice effect rather than removing it, so the plan reports the official-score difference between the two orders as a study output. The retest literature it cites puts practice effects at about d = 0.24 to 0.26 per re-administration, and it expects format familiarity without item overlap to sit well below that.
records.against: Accounts differ on whether the order design was new: the package's response says the review's claim that counterbalancing was missing was a factual error (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/red-team/RED_TEAM_RESPONSE.md`).

records.title: Coherent texts to learn, cold texts to test
records.statement: Sequence the texts learners study so taught knowledge recurs and builds, and keep unseen, unrelated texts whose answers were never taught for tests and transfer items, where the same overlap would be a leak.
records.example: Readers of a coherent text set gained 5.59 concept idea-units against 2.63 for unrelated texts over six texts in three days.
records.detail: An outside review of a Grade 3 reading course found it sequenced as a Lexile staircase rather than a knowledge progression, with assessment passages kept off the taught topics by design, so knowledge was engineered out; it asked for learning texts in which taught knowledge recurs and compounds, with cold, non-overlapping passages kept for the test. In a randomised study, readers of a coherent text set gained 5.59 vs 2.63 concept idea-units (η²=.32) over six texts in three days.
records.against: The study took place in one rural school with fourth graders reading on grade level, and its gains were in topic knowledge, vocabulary and retelling of a new text; its comprehension-question scores were not significant. a project note warned that knowledge-building can be gamed if later questions become answerable from earlier lessons, and the store rates the transfer of knowledge as near-domain at best (η²=.09). Knowledge carried forward can answer a test item: in one historical gate run, an item no blind solver answered (0/3) was answered every time with the earlier lessons' texts (3/3) and was swapped, though a later replay with a newer model answered it blind as well. The later design's separation was verified only at design level, so whether it holds at run time was unverified. When the target test mixes unrelated texts, topic coherence is itself a scaffold to fade before the test, gradually rather than at a cliff (`grade3-reading/artifacts/g5_build_2026_07_02/approval_clean.md`). The study had 59 readers in one rural school over a 3-day intervention, its comprehension-question measure was null and unreliable, and it is not clear whether texts that merely share a topic would do the same (`ti-courseplans-audit/docs/reading-science/SYNTHESIS.qmd`); the BrainLift itself notes that knowledge transfer is near-domain at best (η²=.09). The study had 59 on-grade readers in one rural school over a three-day intervention, its comprehension-question measure was unreliable, and it is unclear whether texts that merely share a topic work the same way (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/reading-science/SYNTHESIS.qmd`, lines 186-189). The course plans add that what carries over to a cold text is operations, vocabulary and format fluency, not topic knowledge: "Topic knowledge is the vehicle, never the cargo" (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/practice-layer-spec.md`, lines 125-128).

records.title: Code checks before a model picks
records.statement: Let a model judge choose only among items that already pass the code checks, and keep it as a selector only if, on saved candidates, it beats taking the first valid item.
records.example: On one saved archive of 15 rows, the model selector passed 13, the same as taking the first valid item.
records.detail: Selector calibration on saved AP candidates found that when invalid candidates reached the model selector, a fluent but invalid question set could beat the one that actually passed, so the rule became code filters first, with the model a selector and not a rescue path. On one saved archive of 15 rows the model selector passed 13, the same as taking the first valid candidate, so it was kept audit-only until a larger calibration proves a lift. records.title: Fix the key, then explain it
records.statement: Fix an item's structure and answer key first, write its explanations against that fixed key, and check that every explanation, hint and feedback line matches the item's actual options and key.
records.detail: A distilled report on one AP generator calls two-stage generation its load-bearing pattern: the structure and key are fixed first and the explanations written against them, which keeps an explanation from contradicting the key (`k_12_social_studies_distilled.md`, lines 44 and 73). Generating multiple-answer items in one stage gave bad answer counts until two-stage generation plus validation fixed it (line 64). The AP evaluator's rubric fails an item whose explanations, hints or feedback describe options or values that are not there, and its first checklist asks whether explanations match the key and options (`mcq_evaluation.txt`, line 85; `_base_evaluation.txt`, line 66). That generator's headline scores were graded by the model family that wrote the items (line 10 of the same report), so this is design evidence, not a measured lift.
records.against: The pattern was proven only for some item types: "Match/fill-in/article were less proven and flagged for more validation" (`k_12_social_studies_distilled.md`, line 49).

evidence.quote: - This prevents the model from generating an explanation that contradicts the answer key.
- Use two-stage generation for answer-bearing item types: lock structure/key first, generate explanations second.

records.title: Certify with an independent judge
records.statement: Nothing that wrote an item, picked it or was optimised against certifies it: confirm it with a check from a different model family that took no part in any of those, on fresh items, verify that independence from the build record, and read a gain the independent check doesn't share as gaming.
records.example: Drafts picked best of eight by one grader passed 92.3% on that grader and 49.2% on a held-out judge.
records.detail: In one AP generator, a 95.2% benchmark came from the writer's model family grading its own questions; the project filed it as design evidence, its rule is never to trust a self-grade as certification, and its notes say a self-grade of 90% against an outside 60% makes the 90% meaningless (`k_12_social_studies_distilled.md`, lines 10, 60 and 72). In another run the grader's own score chose the best of several drafts: on the same 297 prompts it passed 92.3% of the winners and a held-out judge 49.2%, a 43.1-point gap (`analytics.md`, lines 41, 46, 184 and 185). A verification spec, citing a published self-refine study, warned that small models tend to answer "yes, this is correct" to checks on their own flawed drafts (`02_R42_CoVe_DBQ_spec.md`, line 174).
records.against: Self-verification did help a large model in a published study, by 15.5 FACTSCORE points on biographies with a 65B model (`02_R42_CoVe_DBQ_spec.md`, line 22). Much of the 43.1-point gap came from two item types the held-out judge failed outright, 0 of 30 where the grader passed 70-100%, which the report says that judge could not yet score; on the other three types it agreed with the grader 70-93% of the time, and the report also notes the grader's lean towards passing (`analytics.md`, lines 46, 64 and 65). an earlier call in the reading project held that re-checking items both graders had passed was redundant; an independent check is only as good as its calibration, since the same audited items had blind accuracy 1.0 under one blind solver and about 0.0 under another; and the AP notes take the top-scored of several drafts to correlate with being genuinely better even when the grader is noisy. A different family may share the same bias: in a study summarised in the reading project, different models converged on a difficulty ranking that diverged from human rankings. the evaluation notes hold that keeping the highest-scored of five also averages out the judge's noise and correlates with being genuinely better even if the noise is high (`icloud-work/ML learnings/evaluation_methodology.md`). The target judge must still be measured as well: "if you're not running every result through the same grader our task is scored on, you'll think you're improving while not improving the metric." (~/Library/Mobile Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/work/aptraining/workspace/EXTERNAL_AGENT_BRIEF.md, 113) The 97.37% and the 20% differ in two ways at once, fresh objectives and no selection, so that pair doesn't isolate the effect of selection. The larger gap is confounded: on one day self-grading passed 56% where an independent model passed 9.1% (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/docs/archive/HOLISTIC_REVIEW_2026-02-19.md`, lines 202-203), but the project put part of the 9.1% down to a different question batch and JSON parsing issues (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/docs/archive/CLAUDE_VS_GEMINI_EVAL.md`, lines 80-82). On the same 14 items the self-grader was only slightly more lenient, 4 of 14 against 3 of 14 (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/docs/archive/CLAUDE_CROSS_EVAL_REPORT.md`, line 17), and a manual review of 30 items on 17 February 2026 concluded: "The problem is NOT "Gemini grading Gemini too leniently" - it's the **EVALUATOR being TOO STRICT**." (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/docs/archive/CLAUDE_MANUAL_REVIEW.md`, line 10). The independent judge was never itself scored against person-labelled items, and the held-out-judge check is a plan whose result is not in this evidence. The 11-item case doesn't isolate family: the same-family benchmark grades instructional quality and never ran a blind solve, so family and check type are confounded, and an audit comparing two solvers concluded that blind-solve calibration matters more than judge identity alone. a 28% figure from the same work was traced to four bugs in the evaluation harness (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0064-insight-stimulus-provenance-unlock.qmd`, line 36), so the binding grader's number needs the same scrutiny. A different family is not enough on its own: a weak different-family solver over-credited items that a stronger one caught (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0235-g5-course-build-pipeline-2026-06-23-to-06-30.qmd`, lines 67-69), and every label in the tuning hand-off came from one solver family (the same file, lines 188-189). The same-family judge also had no test of text-dependence at all (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/pr-proposals/ti-courseplans-standards/staged/courses/g5-reading/llm/LLM_SPEC.qmd`, lines 111-112), so its misses cannot be put down to model family alone. The plan was a draft, and every blind-solve label came from one solver family, with no two-family agreement measured. One note puts the inflation at 43 points ('Goodhart contamination (IB-aggregator → judge says 49% vs IB 92%, 43pp gap).', `icloud-work/aptraining/.agent/memory/MEMORY.md`, line 185), but in the run behind those numbers (49.16% against 92.26% on 297 items) the held-out judge's single generic rubric scored 0 of 30 on every multi-part item type, and that run's note calls it 'Format mismatch, not Goodhart.' (`project_stacked_decode_RAG_judge_result.md`, lines 21-22, 46, 53); the size of the inflation was not measured. The second rubric in the 20-point comparison was later retired as the canonical judge (`icloud-work/aptraining/.agent/memory/MEMORY.md`, line 73). A second judge can fail for its own reasons: one with a generic single-prompt rubric scored 0/30 on every question-set and document-based cell, which the project read as a rubric too generic for multi-part outputs rather than bad items, so it kept that judge as a check on simple formats only, until it has rubrics fit to each format. Unmeasured: such rejections 'are rejected on reasoning, not on measurement' (~/Projects/shadow/bench/docs/brainlift.md line 92), and when the probe was added only its fail-open path had been verified live (~/Projects/shadow/bench, git commit e435432, lines 22-24). A stricter version removed good items: insisting on clean passes cut useful candidates that had some past failures but strong fresh behaviour. A model judge choosing among six drafts did help another item type, from 22/30 to 28/30, but that compared it with a stored bank rather than a single draft, and 22 against 23 of 25 is a one-item gap. The evaluator's own regression set was pruned by the judge's results instead, removing every item that mismatched its expected category or errored across 10 hardening runs to steady a 0.99 gate, and a later change to the same regression suite called pruning whack-a-mole.

records.title: Close the class, not the instance
records.statement: Treat each defect, finding, rejection or review comment as a class: search everything made the same way, turn it into a standing check for the whole class (or a dated rule where code can't check it) that asserts what the student experiences, show it fires before the fix, run it on every lesson, and count new against repeat classes.
records.example: 39 checks were added in 5 weeks, yet one defect class took seven separate commits.
records.detail: The reading project's QA notes found that 39 checks were added in 5 weeks (7-10 a week) while the same defect classes kept coming back, one of them across seven separate commits, and a later formatting commit silently reverted an earlier pronunciation fix. What converged was closing a finding only when its whole class has an executable check of what the student experiences, and counting new against repeat classes in every round report. When one instance of a text-to-speech trap turned up, the rule became a census of every instance in the course file rather than assuming a one-off, and a give-away cue rule was swept over every grade.

Some renders voice such an opening anyway, so each case's transcript is checked rather than assumed (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0200-content-audio-review-traps.qmd`). records.title: Harder instructions, weaker adherence
records.statement: Writer models keep to constraints less reliably as instructions get harder, and whether giving a writer only the rules its task needs, not the whole rulebook, fixes that is untested.

records.title: Few questions during reading
records.statement: Keep questions during reading few and at natural breaks, because frequent ones can cut young readers' recall of what they don't ask about, and measure recall of the whole text when changing them.
records.example: In one study, Grade 4 recall of untargeted information fell from .30 with no questions to .07 with questions during reading.
records.detail: A research-boundary review checked a cited experiment in which 240 students, 60 each in Grades 4/7/10 and college, met 14 written causal questions per story during reading, after reading or not at all (Van den Broek et al. 2001, https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.93.3.521; `grade3-reading/artifacts/feedback-devfactory-2026-09-10/analysis-current-courses/RESEARCH-BOUNDARIES.md`, section 2). The quoted fall from .30 to .07 is Grade 4 recall of untargeted information, not overall comprehension, and the college benefits concerned targeted information. The review concludes that frequent unsupported interruptions can be costly for younger readers, and that a change of timing should compare equal-content versions and measure both whole-story understanding and targeted learning.
records.against: After-reading questions also lowered that recall (.16 against .30), readers could not look back while answering, and the review says the study does not establish a ban on every mid-text check, especially sparse checks at coherent boundaries with the text available (the same file, lines 27-31).

records.statement: When text or a model answer appears bit by bit, reveal it in whole words or chunks in step with the explanation, not by slow letter-by-letter tracing.
records.example: In one study, whole-word appearance beat letter tracing on recall with d=.97.
records.detail: A research-boundary review checked two studies an outside review cited (`grade3-reading/artifacts/feedback-devfactory-2026-09-10/analysis-current-courses/RESEARCH-BOUNDARIES.md`, section 1). In a paper comparing fonts and reveal styles in narrated videos, Study 1, with 12 university adults and pseudowords, found whole-word appearance beat tracing on recall, d=.97 (Ram & Zhao 2022); a study of diagrams drawn during narration, four experiments with 484 college students, found conditional transfer benefits, not a universal effect (Fiorella & Mayer 2016, https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000065). The review concludes that progressive modelling with synchronized explanation is plausible, that slow letter tracing that obstructs reading should be avoided, and that a chunked reveal is a reasonable prototype.
records.against: Both studies used adults and non-reading tasks; with typeface held constant, whole-word against tracing was d=.74 with corrected p=.077/.076, a trend rather than a significant contrast; and the paper compares no single-word reveal against chunks and sets no child-specific speed (the same file, lines 17-21).

evidence.quote: **Design conclusion:** progressive modelling with synchronized explanation is plausible.
Whole-word appearance beat tracing on recall in Study1, d=.97.
**Design conclusion:** avoid slow letter tracing that obstructs reading; chunked reveal is a reasonable prototype.

records.statement: No surface feature may single out the key: keep options alike in length, grammar, register and scope, so the key is never the longest, shortest, most specific, most hedged, odd one out or only option sharing a distinctive word with the stem or source, use no absolute words or 'all/none of the above', and check lengths in code, item by item and across the set, moving reasoning from the key into its feedback where it runs long.

records.title: Tuning finds what the score misses
records.statement: A writer tuned or selected against a score converges on whatever the score does not test, so anything a question must have, such as needing its text, has to be part of what selects the writer.
records.example: Tuned against a structure-only score, a writer produced a question rated 1.0 that a solver answered without its passage every time.
records.detail: In the reading project's tuning run, the reward measured structural quality only and had no concept of passage-dependency; it plateaued at ~0.14 once the writer had converged to structurally valid leaked questions. The spec concluded that the two quality dimensions are orthogonal and both must be in the reward signal. The follow-up directive was to optimize the course, not the item: a course where every item scores 1.0 but 90% is blind-solvable is a failed course, as a question scored 1.0 with a blind-solve rate of 100% showed. In the AP work, a fix that raised a question set's score did it by removing the stimulus, which skipped the grader's leak probe.

records.example: Under the first gate, 97% of multiple-choice items were answered without the passage, against 0% of matching items.

records.title: Match face, voice and motion
records.statement: Give a synthetic human on screen a face, voice and motion that match, since a mismatch between them, more than realism, is what makes it read as fake.
records.detail: The Grade 9 video research found that moving, speaking synthetic humans still read as fake, and that the trigger is a mismatch between face, voice and motion more than the level of realism: a human-realistic face with a synthetic voice, or the reverse, was rated eerier than a fully synthetic or fully human pairing (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0202-g9-othello-video-research-fake-ai-attention.qmd`; `grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0248-g9-video-research-full-files.qmd`; Mitchell et al. 2011). Across 2023 to 2025 studies such figures showed no reliable learning loss but a real engagement and comfort loss: with 108 undergraduates performance was the same and video engagement higher with a person (Arkün-Kocadere & Çağlar Özhan 2024), and in another study an AI voice with an AI face beat every other pairing on retention, the fully human one included (Xu et al. 2025). A meta-analysis found that an agent's presence and role matter while its realism of rendering does not (Castro-Alonso et al. 2021), another study found more realism brought more looking but less learning (Li et al. 2024), and the plan that followed chose a stylized, non-photoreal figure with its voice matched to its face.
records.against: realism itself is contested: in a science-communication framing a realistic avatar was rated significantly more trustworthy than a stylized one (n=491; Baake, Schmitt & Metag 2025); in a small eye-tracking study high behavioural fidelity raised social presence and transfer; one study found cartoon-like agents scored worst on students' valence and arousal; and a controlled study found no significant differences in satisfaction or trust between AI-generated and recorded human video (Xu et al. 2025) (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0248-g9-video-research-full-files.qmd`).

evidence.quote: **Moving, speaking synthetic humans still read as fake.** The trigger is a mismatch between face, voice and motion, more than the level of realism
**AI presenters show no reliable learning loss, but a real engagement and comfort loss**
Presence and role matter; realism of rendering does not.

records.title: Real texts, honestly labelled
records.statement: For literature, prefer an authentic, well-written text, split into parts where needed, to fiction a model writes, and label any adapted, retold or machine-written text as such on the page where it is read, so no one takes it for the original or for a real source.
records.detail: A 2026-08-19 decision in the reading project put authentic fiction first: machine-written fiction "is never going to be great", so real texts split into parts are the priority, and units built on synthetic prose were flagged as a rebuild risk (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0198-meetings-decisions-timeline-0819-1001.qmd`). The project's cold test passages are machine-written and labelled humanApproved:false, and its insight note warns never to relabel them as real (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0064-insight-stimulus-provenance-unlock.qmd`).

records.title: No live self-view while learning
records.statement: Keep a live view of the learner's own face out of a lesson, because seeing oneself can raise appearance anxiety and lower recall.
records.example: Across 3 experiments with university students, self-view raised appearance anxiety, and that anxiety lowered lecture recall.
records.detail: The Grade 9 idea research reports a peer-reviewed paper of 3 experiments with 171, 124 and 224 university students in which camera-on with self-view raised social appearance anxiety most, and that anxiety, not camera status itself, mediated lower lecture recall. records.statement: Where there is time, explain through a dialogue that answers a learner's questions, or by refuting the wrong idea, rather than by straight exposition.

records.title: One process, falling support
records.statement: Modelling, guided practice and independent practice should run one skill under the same step names through to the recap, with support that only falls, so the stages still read as one process with their labels stripped: the model shows the thinking rather than the answer, guided practice is a part-finished task the student completes rather than a hint, and independent work does the same operation on new material with the least help.
records.example: A deterministic lint catches all three ways this failed in one review round: the answer shown as the model, a hint as the guided step, and a switch of skill as the independent one.
records.detail: The reading course standard calls the I-do, we-do, you-do routine one process practised three ways, never three activities, and its acceptance test is that with the labels stripped the three still teach the same process at decreasing support (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/instruction-quality-standard.md`, lines 13-25). A review round found all three ways this fails, and a deterministic lint now catches them, among 6 of the 10 failure shapes that round found (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/handoffs-2026-07-13/course-eval-layer/evaluator-spec.md`, lines 69-71). A clean-room review found independent work returning to the model's own example and evidence instead of new evidence (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/standards/student-course-quality/evidence/AGENT-ENTRYPOINT-CLEAN-ROOM-G3-U4-L1-2026-08-06.qmd`, lines 57-58). Guided work leaves the substantive step unfinished (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/standards/student-course-quality/sources/review-hub/course-insights-d7f57fb/ATOMS.json`, line 245), and the independent step is never more scaffolded than the guided one by default: extra help there is offered after a first miss (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/skills/g3-reading-red-team/references/feedback-2026-08-06-addendum.md`, lines 332-337).
records.against: One lesson ships a gap-fill on its independent step by default, a known inversion accepted on instruction after it was argued (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/skills/g3-reading-red-team/references/feedback-2026-08-06-addendum.md`, lines 340-345). The standard also lets the surface format change between stages only while the operation stays demonstrably the same (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/standards/student-course-quality/versions/1.0.0/STANDARD.qmd`, line 317). These are one project's rulings and design standard, not a measured effect on learning, and the modelling split has one exception, where composing a summary is itself the child's work. A later ruling accepted keeping the same question from the model to the guided step, against a claim that each stage needs a different question, with only the independent step moving to a fresh one: "The I-do→we-do handoff keeping the same question is the house release pattern; the" (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/artifacts/g5-course/G3-U1-L4-RESIDUAL-ADJUDICATION-2026-08-21.md`, line 24). The lint checks only the declared structure; whether a model's trace is a real think-aloud rather than an answer reveal is a judged check, advisory until it is calibrated (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/handoffs/g3-reading-v2-feedback-2026-07-16/tooling/ti-courseplans-2169d1f/scripts/lane-tools/op-lint/README.md`, lines 21-23). the Grade 9 design specification lets confident students skip ahead: a quick check at the start of guided practice lets them move straight on (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0204-g9-year-9-ela-lesson-design-specification.qmd`, line 326). Only the shape is checked in code: the reading project's semantic lints stayed advisory after a judge trial ended NO-GO, so whether a think-aloud shows real thinking is not checked by machine. In that case the unmodelled task was objective, had a three-try ladder and revealed its answer at the floor, which the register counts as mitigation (`GAPS-2026-09-11.md`, lines 34-35); and the value analysis says none of it is evidence from a child (`L6-VALUE.md`, lines 3-5). The lesson designs had no guided stage of their own: "design docs go straight from Modelling Moment to Independent Task — they contain no we-do." The rebuilt lesson added one, and the spec keeps one modelled move for good: "This modelling never fades." The study compared less and more experienced learners, not the same learners over time.

records.title: Assume only what was taught and kept
records.statement: A lesson may assume, or tell students they have seen, only what earlier lessons in its sequence taught and the learner still holds fluently enough on a later day to leave working memory free, so record what each lesson builds on and seeds, keep every keystone later lessons need, and check the whole sequence in code, failing any lesson the check can't find.
records.detail: The reading project's instruction spec makes it a code-checked invariant that a lesson assumes only what earlier lessons taught, and counts an anchor as available only after a delayed ≥24h retest passed on new parallel items, so one first taught the same day, or present but not fluent, is not met (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/instruction-modes-spec.md`, section 4). A committed negative fixture, a lesson assuming knowledge no earlier lesson added, was scored as individually fine by the per-lesson quality evaluator and was caught only by the cross-lesson invariant (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/handoffs-2026-07-13/course-eval-layer/evaluator-spec.md`). The course standard asks that each prerequisite be established, activated, retaught, newly introduced or routed through a tested on-ramp (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/standards/student-course-quality/versions/2.0.0/GOLDEN-CHECKLIST.qmd`, Q015); the curriculum BrainLift says a prerequisite that is met but not automated enough to free working memory makes the target skill unteachable (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/feedback/feedback1/Curriculum & Knowledge BrainLift.md`), and the project's curriculum reference gives soft prerequisites a fluency threshold rather than a binary met or unmet (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/skills/train-teacher/references/curriculum-architecture.md`).

records.title: Practise facts and schemas differently
records.statement: Practise a stable fact with brief, frequent retrieval that tapers off, and practise understanding that depends on a schema by retrieving it, getting feedback and then using it in a new task, such as explaining, comparing or placing it.

records.title: Block first, mix after a later retest

records.detail: The reading project's practice spec keeps a skill in blocked practice while it is being acquired and makes it eligible for interleaving only after a delayed (≥24h) retest passed on new parallel items; completion on the day of release never qualifies, because same-day testing measures working memory, not learning (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/practice-layer-spec.md`). records.title: Each wrong option a named misconception
records.statement: Build each wrong option from a different, named misconception or predictable error that students really make, such as a wrong time, place, cause or actor, in the same category and grain as the key, so that choosing it shows what was misunderstood, record which error it targets, and give it feedback that corrects that error, since an uncorrected lure can teach the error and an option nobody would pick is only filler.
records.example: One audit found only about 7% of choice items naming the misconception a wrong option targets.
records.detail: An assessment BrainLift used as feedback for the reading courses calls distractor and feedback quality coupled decisions: misconception-based distractors carry the highest risk of the negative suggestion effect, and Butler & Roediger (2008) showed that feedback largely neutralises it (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/feedback/feedback3/WF - Assessment  Feedback Brain - 260624-200115.md`, line 1991). The courses' instruction-quality standard makes each distractor the answer a named misconception picks, with feedback that names it (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/instruction-quality-standard.md`, lines 129-130), yet an assessment memo found only ~7% of choice items (15 of 48 lessons) naming the specific misconception (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g3-reading/iteration-2/approval-package-v2/sources/ASSESSMENT-QUALITY-MEMO.md`, line 44). An adversarial review's checklist calls strong misconception distractors with no feedback teaching the error, and a fourth option no misconception would pick filler, worse than three options (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/skills/course-red-team/references/finding-taxonomy.md`, lines 160 and 166); the BrainLift agrees that a weak fourth distractor is worse than none (line 2006).
records.against: in an exploit study, options parallel in form but obviously wrong to a knowledgeable reader still passed the judge's distractor checks, and a step that rebuilt weak distractors gave no gain in pass rate over 5 samples. The quiz pipeline's plausibility rule: "If the distractor has ANY connection to the passage OR question, it PASSES (score=1)" (`~/Library/Mobile Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/work/incept/aplit-quiz-generation/lit-question-qc.json`, line 8). Among near misses, the project's own fix list counted 30 distractor problems and rated fixing them harder, needing content work, and low in impact (`icloud-work/incept/nova_forge/README.md`, line 303). One run report proposed the opposite for easy items, in a prompt it recommended for the writer: '- Have obviously wrong distractors (for MCQ)' (`icloud-work/evaluator/docs/reports/BENCHMARK_RUN4_REPORT.md`, line 326). No student responses were ever collected, so the guidance's own test of a working wrong option, chosen by at least 5% of test-takers, was never applied, and plausibility was judged only by models (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/docs/analysis/best_practices.md`). For a single-skill standard, wrong options that share a failure category are normal good design (`icloud-work/inceptbench-main/src/inceptbench/prompts/question/closed_ended_evaluation.txt`, line 600). The misconception list reaches the judge only on the unmerged AP branch; the current AP context has no misconception field (`icloud-work/inceptbench-main/src/inceptbench/evaluators/base.py`, lines 796-817). The spec is inconsistent on the count: it says each item has exactly 3 distractors, one of each, then lists four types, while the item bank's gate asks for four types present. The benchmark's link between such distractors and passing is an observation, not a test. The research's minimum effective feedback is showing the correct answer, while the reading course never reveals a single-select item's answer after a set number of tries, because a short option list lets the child eliminate their way to it (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0183-copy-question-quality-rulings.qmd`); whether eliminating to the right option corrects a lure as well as being shown it has not been measured here. A planned test of misconception-seeded options, to be replicated on 150 items if distractor quality rose 3 points, has no recorded result in the files read (~/Library/Mobile Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/work/aptraining/helpers/data/output/path_e/path_e_build_notes.md, line 42). In that strand the tags were assigned by a model ("deterministic dose assembler + LLM misconception tagging", `grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0008-alpha-courses-repo.qmd`, lines 135-136), and an enum validator checks that each option carries a tag from the list, not that the tag is right. The grade 3 profile also requires at least 4 options on every multiple-choice item and no true/false item in the mastery pool, since a yes/no is a 50/50 guess, while the same criteria drop to 3 options rather than add a weak fourth, so where no fourth real error exists the two rules conflict (`ti-courseplans-audit/skills/g3-reading-red-team/references/dimensions/D5-assessment-item-construction.md`). Quick are-you-still-reading checks are treated differently: one story design keeps them free of trick distractors, while the science designs build theirs to the same rule, misconception distractor included. The general bar is softer: an incorrect but content-plausible option that could tempt a non-expert student is acceptable, not a failure, and the SAT math rule asks for only one such option.

records.title: Refute the misconception learners bring
records.statement: When learners commonly bring a wrong belief to a topic, draw it out once at the start as a prediction on the question the lesson answers, refute it and don't voice it again, because a clear correct explanation alone can leave it standing; a misconception that poor teaching produced is fixed by changing the explanation instead.
records.example: In one study, refuting the misconception beat a concise correct explanation on immediate gains by about d 0.79.
records.detail: A short-video BrainLift in the course plans holds that a clear explanation can produce the feeling of understanding while the misconception survives, and that a video should open by confronting a documented misconception when it is central, citing refutation ≈ d 0.79 and dialogue ≈ d 0.83 over concise correct exposition on immediate conceptual gains (Muller 2008) (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g7-science/brainlifts/video-generation-human-v0.2.md`, lines 113-118). A generic instruction BrainLift sorts misconceptions by source: instinctive ones are taught explicitly with contrastive material and revisited, while ones produced by poor instruction are not foregrounded but designed out of the explanation (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/feedback/feedback1/Generic Instruction BrainLift.md`, lines 60-61).
records.against: The BrainLift scopes the evidence to immediate gains in undergraduates where the misconception is central, not a proven delayed-retention benefit (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g7-science/brainlifts/video-generation-human-v0.2.md`, lines 117-119); and in a study of short narrated videos, refutation text structures largely made no significant difference against an expository one (Schroeder et al. 2022, https://doi.org/10.1177/07356331211070534). The study is cited as a dissertation with no DOI or URL in these files, and introductory or overview lessons are exempt and may open on plain curiosity (`ti-courseplans-audit/skills/video-red-team/references/rubric.md`).

evidence.quote: When a documented misconception is central, open by confronting it.
A clear explanation can produce the feeling of understanding while the misconception survives.
concise correct exposition on immediate conceptual gains (Muller 2008: refutation ≈ d 0.79, dialogue ≈ d 0.83) [20]. Scope: immediate, undergraduate, misconception-central
teach explicitly with contrastive material; expect to revisit.
don't foreground — fix the explanation so it isn't produced.
A clear explanation that never engages the prior belief produces confident non-learning (Muller: clear-only exposition barely moved scores; misconception-first nearly doubled the gain).
The wrong belief is voiced at most once, at the open, and never rehearsed/scolded in the body
where the teaching atom owns a named misconception, the opener must ELICIT the intuitive wrong belief ONCE (as an invited prediction / reasonable guess), then resolve it against that tension.
They must be the same conceptual question, and the positive body must explicitly resolve the prediction raised at the open.
If deleting the hook leaves the body teaching an unrelated objective unchanged, the hook is misaligned.
Intro/overview atoms are exempt (curiosity hook ok).

records.title: Hard for the right reason
records.statement: Make an item's difficulty come from the knowledge or reasoning it tests, such as more steps, synthesis, a subtle distinction or a plausible confusion, never from its label, rare or untaught words, hard syntax, negatives, obscure facts, padded reading load, a clumsy way of answering or extra help in the stem, and if plainer wording that tests the same thing would make it easier, remove that difficulty.
records.detail: The assessment BrainLift holds that an item whose difficulty can't be explained by the knowledge it targets is almost certainly measuring a mix of construct and noise, and that hardness from convoluted language, tricky negatives and obscure contexts is an invalid obstacle, not rigour (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/feedback/feedback3/WF - Assessment  Feedback Brain - 260624-200115.md`, lines 2366-2367); its diagnostic section adds that an item should not punish students who know the material but are tripped up by wording (line 398). In the Grade 3 course an ordering item shipped as a menu of position numbers per event, which taxed exactly the working memory the item existed to measure comprehension with; it became drag-and-drop with its own check, and the build rules now say to match the gesture to the shape of the answer (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g3-reading/iteration-3/BUILD-RULES.md`, lines 757-766).
records.against: An earlier lesson in the same project said the reverse, that hard questions must require recall, not reading, and that scaffolding makes hard questions medium (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/docs/archive/ITERATION_ANALYSIS.md`). One review allowed that heavy scaffolding might be acceptable in a practice item for struggling students (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/docs/analysis/evaluation_audit.md`). The 86%-to-62% drop came from a retrain that also regressed other item types, so it is not a clean test of labels (`icloud-work/ap-social-studies-generator/HANDOFF-finetune-status.md`). Multi-step prompts where each step drives a different decision are not flagged, and a first step that asks for a member of a closed grammatical category is exempt (`icloud-work/inceptbench-main/src/inceptbench/prompts/question/_base_evaluation.txt`, lines 151 and 156). The difficulty verdicts were a model judge's opinion with no learner data, and the pattern swung between runs: the run that broke hard items fixed easy ones, from 27% to 68%. records.title: A difficulty set before use is a prior
records.statement: Treat any difficulty, threshold or cut score set before learners have answered as a labelled prior: estimate difficulty from item features or calibrated anchors rather than a model's own rating, record its method, sample size and uncertainty, set no cut score on it, and replace it with live response data.
records.example: A model's direct rating tracks real difficulty at about r 0.4 to 0.6, against up to 0.87 for a feature model trained on calibrated items.
records.detail: A diagnostic BrainLift worked through on AP courses notes that estimating one item's difficulty with reasonable precision needs at minimum 100-200 responses, that at about 10 students per course it takes 10-20 cohorts to reach 100, and so parameters must come from judgment and structural defaults (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/feedback/feedback3/WF - Assessment  Feedback Brain - 260624-200115.md`, lines 382-384). Its cold-start section, drawing on published studies, ranks a model's direct rating as the weakest approach (often r ≈ 0.4–0.6), behind feature-based models (r ≈ 0.7–0.87 with ≥100 calibrated items) and placement against 3–5 calibrated anchors, distrusts predictions that swing under small wording changes, and requires every pre-use value to carry a provenance label such as 'pre-use predicted, N=0' (lines 3172-3196). The reading courses' standard says the same: predicted difficulty is a prior with method, population, provenance and uncertainty, which live data must eventually replace (`~/Projects/grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/standards/student-course-quality/sources/knowledge-bot/kb-0164-g3-v2-feedback-agent-routing.qmd`, lines 97-98).

records.title: Placement and gap-finding are different diagnostics
records.statement: Treat placement and gap-finding as different diagnostics, since placement in an ordered course needs only a short binary search while finding gaps needs sampling across the course, one gap at a time.
records.example: A binary search finds the starting unit of a 9-unit course in 3-4 items.
records.detail: A diagnostic BrainLift written around AP courses, one of the assessment BrainLifts given to the reading course plans, separates placement, a search for one cut-point on a roughly ordered course, from hole-filling, which assumes no order and needs the full knowledge-mapping machinery at 40-60+ items and 15-30 minutes (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/feedback/feedback3/WF - Assessment  Feedback Brain - 260624-200115.md`). For a 9-unit course the search takes 3-4 items (log₂(9) ≈ 3.2). For gaps it advises finding one, sizing it, filling it and repeating, instead of mapping every hole at once.
records.against: The same BrainLift rules the search out for a course with no sequential structure, which goes straight to full knowledge-mapping, and it sizes a placement two ways: 10-15 items and 5 minutes in one place, 7-10 items and 3-5 minutes in another.

evidence.quote: A placement diagnostic can be done in 10-15 items and 5 minutes.
This typically takes 3-4 items for a 9-unit course (log₂(9) ≈ 3.2).
**Insight 6: You don't need to find all the holes at once — find a hole, size it, fill it, repeat.**
Total items: typically 7-10 items. Total time: 3-5 minutes.
If the course genuinely lacks sequential structure (e.g., a collection of independent topics with no progression), this diagnostic is inappropriate — go straight to full knowledge-mapping.

records.title: Knowledge taught together moves together
records.statement: What was taught together tends to be known or missing together, so where a course has few prerequisites, sample a diagnostic by the units things were taught in rather than testing every component.
records.example: At 3 items for each of 400-600+ components, testing every component of an AP course would take 1,200-1,800 items, roughly 10-15 hours.
records.detail: The diagnostic BrainLift argues that components taught in the same unit and the same week have correlated mastery, not because they depend on each other but because the causes of knowing them are shared, so two failed items from one unit should lower the estimate for the whole unit (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/feedback/feedback3/WF - Assessment  Feedback Brain - 260624-200115.md`). It calls this instructional clustering and leans on it in subjects with many components and sparse prerequisite structure, where prerequisite chains cannot carry the inference. A well-decomposed AP course might hold 400-600+ components, and at 3 items each that is 1,200-1,800 items, roughly 10-15 hours of testing.
records.against: This is the BrainLift's statistical argument; nothing in the evidence measures how strongly mastery moves together within a unit.

evidence.quote: KCs taught in the same unit, by the same teacher, in the same week, will be correlated in their mastery status — not because the KCs are logically related, but because the *causes* of knowing or not knowing them are shared.
instructional clustering, which exploits shared exposure history rather than logical dependencies
A well-decomposed AP course might contain 400-600+ knowledge components. At 3 items per KC (a bare minimum for defensible inference), that's 1,200-1,800 items — roughly 10-15 hours of testing.

records.title: A difference must clear the noise
records.statement: Count a difference between versions as real only when it clears the judge's run-to-run spread for that item type, measured item by item by re-scoring the same saved items over several runs, and audit an unexpected win as closely as a loss.
records.example: Three scorings of unchanged outputs varied with a standard deviation of 1.54 points overall but 7-9 points on the document-based type.
records.detail: A three-run probe of the AP judge on unchanged outputs found a standard deviation of 1.54 points overall but 7-9 points on the document-based type, with two types not varying at all, and the same outputs scored 24/30 and 19/30 on two runs, so a difference under 5 points from a single call was not to be trusted (`icloud-work/aptraining/.agent/memory/MEMORY.md`). A routed setup's 92% rested on one lucky 30/30 run of one item type whose rate over three seeds was about 80%, and an earlier single-run score in the 0.9 range proved to be noise when re-run over three seeds (the same file; `icloud-work/aptraining/.agent/memory/BEADS.md`). The project then required three seeds before any single-attempt number, a standard deviation across seeds of 4 points or less before a mean could be read, and an audit of the prompt and output of anything that passed unexpectedly (`icloud-work/aptraining/.agent/PLAN.md`; `icloud-work/aptraining/.agent/memory/PILLARS_2026_05_12.md`).
records.against: Most of the document-based spread was later traced to the pass/fail cut ('DBQ "noise" was ~all threshold artifact', `icloud-work/aptraining/.agent/memory/MEMORY.md`, line 113), and a long-essay type was one of the two that did not vary, so the spread is not simply a matter of length. The spreads come from three runs on one set of saved outputs, so the thresholds are rough: "**Finding (T0, 3 independent IB v2.5.3 runs on identical v29 gens, 2026-04-29):**" (~/Library/Mobile Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/work/aptraining/workspace/comms/from_shadow/2026-04-30T1700Z_comprehensive_lessons_learned.md, 132). Where the spread is zero, any change counts: "- MCQ/LEQ: essentially deterministic (σ=0), any non-zero delta is real" (the same file, 144). Small gains need many items: at 30 items per type a paired test detects differences of about 0.05 or more with 80% power, and smaller ones need 120 or more per type (`icloud-work/aptraining/handover/2026-05-01T1039Z_compass_session_close/03_R41D_implementation.md`). A continuous score also needs a freshly generated baseline, without which several regressions reversed (`icloud-work/aptraining/handover/2026-05-01T1039Z_main_session_close/02_CONSOLIDATED_STATE.md`). And an aggregate can look steady while item types swing: across three seeds the overall rate had a standard deviation under a point while one type passed 6, 7 and 9 of 30 (`icloud-work/aptraining-crystal-copy-20260521/full-copy/aptraining-root/achieved.md`).

records.title: Accept a generator on its worst type
records.statement: Test a generator on every item type it must produce and accept it on its worst type, not its average, because a good score on one type says nothing about another.
records.example: A model whose numbers came from multiple-choice items alone failed to produce parseable document-based items 50% of the time.

The project then set its goal as the minimum over its ten course and item-type cells, not the mean, because an average can hide a regression on the hardest cell (`icloud-work/aptraining/.agent/NORTH_STAR.md`).
records.against: The breakage was concentrated in the most complex type: "Other untrained types (mcq_set, saq, leq) parse OK 86-100% — they're structurally simpler." (`icloud-work/auto-memory-backup/project_v8_mcq_only.md`, line 18).

v8's training data was filtered to MCQ records only (2,821 records, all `question_type=mcq`). When tested on the full 10-cell holdout, v8 produces non-parseable output ~50% of the time on DBQ:
Single-cell results without the 10-cell context can hide DBQ-style failures.
- Cell-balance matters: don't optimize one cell while breaking others. Test on the full eval set, not just the one you're working on.

records.title: Sample a stored pool at random
records.statement: To estimate a single-try or best-of-several rate from a stored pool of scored candidates, sample the pool at random or generate afresh, because the top of a score-sorted list is always the pool's best.
records.example: Read off the top of a score-sorted list, one model's single-try rate came out at 99.11%, which was its best-of-8 rate.
records.detail: In the AP work, each prompt's eight candidate scores were stored sorted best first, so the first entry, or the best of the first two, always returned the best-of-8 score (`icloud-work/aptraining/.agent/memory/feedback_k8_bon_winner_trap_2026_05_11.md`). On one day that mistake was reported twice, as a single-try rate and as a best-of-2 rate, both 99.11%; a fresh single-try run that day scored 82.67% (`icloud-work/aptraining/.agent/memory/FINAL_PLAN_2026_05_11_v3.md`). The rule since is to simulate a smaller pool by sampling stored candidates at random, or to generate afresh (`icloud-work/aptraining/.agent/memory/feedback_k8_bon_winner_trap_2026_05_11.md`).
records.against: none found

evidence.quote: True K=N from K=8 data requires random pair sampling.

records.title: Deduplicate on the full content
records.statement: Deduplicate and count items on their full content, not on an opening prefix or an earlier step's count, because items that open alike need not be duplicates and reported counts can include repeats.
records.example: Hashing only the first 200 characters wrongly marked 34% of distinct records as duplicates.
records.detail: A training-set build hashed the first 200 characters of each record, so different records that open alike, such as multiple-choice items with the same question opening, counted as duplicates: it seemed to hold 37k unique records, a 34% false duplicate rate, until full-content hashing found 56,554 in one source file alone (`training_data_70k.md`, lines 30-33). A source pool reported as about 31 candidates per objective held 12-14 unique documents once deduplicated, because the reported count included repeats across rounds (`feedback_cache_pool_count_vs_unique_doc_count_distinct_2026_06_01.md`, lines 7-9).
records.against: A whole-item hash catches only exact copies; near-duplicates need another test, and the folder has none.

evidence.quote: `build_70k_dataset.py` used MD5 hash of first 200 chars of assistant content for dedup. This caused massive FALSE POSITIVES — many different records share the same first 200 chars (e.g., MCQs with the same question opening). Fixed to use **full content MD5 hash**.
**Before fix:** appeared to have only 37k unique records (34% false dedup rate)
Actual unique-doc pool was 12-14 per KC after dedup, not 31.
**Bug:** Used MD5 hash of first 200 chars of assistant content for deduplication.

This caused massive FALSE POSITIVES. Many different records share the same opening 200 characters:
- MCQs starting with "Which of the following best describes..."
- LEQs starting with "Evaluate the extent to which..."
- DBQs starting with "Using the documents..."

Result: Appeared to have only 37k unique records from what should have been 59k+. A 34% false dedup rate made the dataset look much smaller than it was, and caused us to think we needed to generate more data.
**Fix:** Full content MD5 hash of the entire assistant response.
**After fix:** 56,554 from raft_combined alone were correctly unique. We didn't need to generate anything.

records.title: Misconceptions are not suggestions
records.statement: Don't hand a writer known misconceptions as loose suggestions for wrong options: it may write them into stems and explanations as if they were true.
records.example: Appended to the request as suggested distractors, misconceptions cut passes from 19 of 22 to 14 of 22.

records.title: Read the checker's code first
records.statement: Read the checker's own code to learn exactly what it grades and parses, and match each item type's output structure to it, checked in code before producing at scale.
records.example: Training rows whose part labels were uppercase strings instead of the parser's lowercase nested parts dropped that item type from 90% to 16.7%.

This is the v38 failure mode (262 rows of answer-format anchors → 0/150 parse_ok).

records.title: Does a strict schema cost quality
records.statement: Open question: does forcing a strict output schema on a writer buy structural compliance at the cost of quality in its free-text parts?

records.title: Quote the evidence before the verdict
records.statement: Make a judge quote before it scores: it copies the text each criterion applies to, lists each fault with that quote and the rule it breaks, credits a pass or a required part only on quoted text, and scores only from those quotes, which are required output fields that code checks against the item.

records.title: Code gates catch broken items, not weak ones
records.statement: Code gates catch broken items, not weak ones: hard-block in code only what code detects reliably, such as a broken format or key or a copied answer, keep keyword, length and wording counts advisory, and judge quality separately, since a valid shape says nothing about it.
records.example: A deterministic suite caught 19 of 102 failing items and rejected 22 of 351 passing ones.
records.detail: On 30 scored AP question sets, a stage validator passed 12 of the 14 failing sets and wrongly failed 1 of the 16 passing ones, and its results note concluded that hard gates are a safety layer, not a quality judge, since most failures were semantic rather than schema or leak failures. Its first version also hard-blocked reading-style, source-referential stems and over-blocked known passing items, so the split kept hard gates for schema, missing fields, answer leaks, extreme length and key clustering and made wording flags advisory. A separate probe of a deterministic suite on 461 generated items caught 19 of 102 failures and rejected 22 of 351 passes, and a shape-only acceptance test passed 25 of 25 in 0.006 s while a graded retest of the same service scored 8 of 20.
records.against: A later design hard-rejects on a semantic check before grading: "reject any item whose answer is derivable from the stimulus" (~/Library/Mobile Documents/com~apple~CloudDocs/work/aptraining/workspace/comms/MCQSET_GENERATION_LEVER.md, line 16). The 8 of 20 retest used a thinner generic prompt than the graded specialist solvers (~/Documents/aptraining/den-of-ideation/from_den/2026-05-25T0758Z_BLOCKED_WORKFLOW_GENERIC_MCq_RETEST.md, line 18), so it shows what the shape check missed, not how good the specialists were. The validator figures come from a replay of archived outputs, not fresh generation (~/Documents/aptraining/den-of-ideation/experiments/b0035_mcqset_stage_validator/RESULTS.md, line 7). Used as gates rather than as scores, cheap word checks still catch real cues, such as the absolute words found in 35% of generated items in one review (`icloud-work/k_12_social_studies/python/docs/EVALUATION-RESULTS-2026-02-23.md`).
